newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-REAL ESTATE ADS WEIGH ON WA NEWS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-REAL ESTATE ADS WEIGH ON WA NEWS.

text.p: West Australian Newspapers Holdings Ltd, which publishes Western Australia's largest circulation newspaper, said on Thursday a weak real estate market would continue to weigh on trading conditions.
"I don't see any immediate sign of significant growth," managing director Denis Thompson told Reuters.
WA Newspapers earlier on Thursday posted a 3.3 percent rise in net profit to A$49.43 million for the year ended June 30 and declared a steady 25 cents annual dividend after a 13 cents final.
A depressed real estate market in Western Australia translated into a 0.4 percent decline in net advertising revenue in 1996/97 to A$179.65 million at its flagship West Australian daily newspaper.
The decline was only partly offset by a net increase of 0.5 percent in revenue from circulation to A$53.86 million
The drop occurred despite a series of interest rate cuts in Australia during the year that made home buying more affordable, suggesting deeper economic woes for the state.
"There have been a number of interest rates cuts, but still it's fair to say the major impediment to growth at this stage is the housing sector," Thompson said.
While some observers are indicating housing may be improving, Thompson said he has yet to see the evidence.
"We're not seeing anything right at this moment ... it's pretty much flat where we were for the last few months."
At this point, Thompson said he can do little more than hope for a lift in consumer confidence in the housing sector to improve revenues in advertising.
Flow-on effects from a more buoyant real estate sector would see improvements in retail, employment and other advertising, he said.
Thompson said he was "reasonably happy" with the 3.3 percent growth in profits in, which was recorded with one less trading week than in the previous year.
He said the company was expecting to improve on growth this year, but acknowledged this will depend on the state's economy.
Newsprint costs, which fell by 5.5 percent to A$50.72 million in 1996/97 should fall further this year, which will help the bottom line, Thompson said.
About 70 percent of the group's newsprint is bought under annual fixed-price contracts. The rest, though, is bought in the spot market, where prices are creeping up, Thompson said.
"There seems to be some upward pressure on the spot price, but overall I think we'll still enjoy a better rate year-on-year," Thompson said.
Savings in 1997/98 will come in part from a move toward pagination in the composing sector, which is linked to voluntary job losses, Thompson said.
Cost savings from the shift to full pagination, scheduled to be completed by the end of 1997/98, may fall short of some expectations, he said.
"Everyone had a view that pagination was going to be a huge saving opportunity, but it's nowhere near what everyone thought," Thompson said.
-- Perth bureau 61-8 9221-7111
